data.hypothesis: The split-range parent was correct but its measured mean was nearly the baseline, while the isolated rsqrtf variant was also correct and had a shorter recorded search mean. Applying the rsqrtf-based inverse-cube factor to both split loops tests whether that arithmetic change remains useful when self interactions are skipped by source ranges. The combined candidate is unmeasured; no speedup or correctness is assumed.

memory_lessons.applicability: These are separate search results, not a measurement of the proposed combination or per-size timing. Use the result to motivate the combination, not to predict its outcome.
memory_lessons.claim: The split-range candidate was valid with a 0.00184293 s mean, close to the 0.00184441 s baseline. The isolated rsqrtf candidate was valid with a 0.00100968 s mean and passed all 11 correctness cases, with maximum reported absolute error 1.52587890625e-05. The combined program still requires validation and measurement.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Validate this combination on the full correctness suite, then compare official scored sizes against both standalone candidates.

data.notes: Only src/nbody_kernel.cu changes; launch settings and one-target-per-thread execution remain unchanged. The split ranges continue to omit j=i entirely, avoiding self-term arithmetic for extreme mass. Although the standalone rsqrtf result passed the supplied correctness cases, this combination still needs controller validation, including coincident positions and extreme mass.
transformations: Retain the split ascending source ranges [0, i) and (i, n), so j=i is excluded without evaluating its interaction.
In both source loops, replace sqrtf(distSq) and division by distSq * dist with an rsqrtf-based inverse-cube factor; retain target-mass multiplication and the final force-per-target-mass update.
Preserve one target per thread, the current launch configuration, and all other integration and output behavior.
